vignette:
Kofi speaks of his old life with a quiet reverence, as if describing a man he once knew but can no longer find. Before the attack, his world was measured in yards of fabric and the steady rhythm of his sewing machine. At 31, he was one of the most sought-after tailors in the market district, his stall a vibrant hub of color and conversation. He took pride in his hands, in the way they could transform a simple bolt of wax print cloth into a sharp suit or an elegant gown. The hum of the market, the haggling, the laughter, the scent of grilled fish from a nearby vendor-this was the soundtrack to a life he had built with precision and care.

That life ended on a Tuesday. He remembers the heat of the afternoon and the specific shade of blue of the fabric he was cutting for a wedding dress. He was arguing playfully with the bride's mother over the price of the lace trim when the world dissolved into a flash of white light and a sound that felt like it tore the air apart. He doesn't remember being thrown, only the sudden, shocking silence that followed, a silence quickly filled by screams. When he came to, his stall was gone, replaced by a crater of splintered wood and scorched earth. The beautiful blue fabric was a tattered, blackened rag clinging to a piece of twisted metal. He saw things that day he does not speak of, images that have burned themselves behind his eyes.

In the first few months, everyone called him lucky. He had escaped with only a deep gash on his forearm and temporary deafness in one ear. His family helped him set up a small workspace in a room at his brother's house. He told himself he would be fine, that he was a survivor. But the market's soundtrack had followed him home, twisted into something monstrous. The friendly roar of a motorcycle in the street was no longer just a motorcycle; it was the prelude to an explosion that made him dive for the floor, his heart hammering against his ribs. The smell of his sister's cooking oil heating in the pan sent a wave of nausea and terror through him, reminding him of the acrid smoke that had choked him.

Sleep offered no escape. He would wake up clawing at his sheets, drenched in sweat, the screams from that day still echoing in his ears. During the day, a heavy, suffocating blanket of numbness settled over him. The joy he once found in his craft vanished. His hands, once so steady and sure, now trembled. Threading a needle became an insurmountable task. He would sit before his sewing machine for hours, the silence in the room deafening, unable to make the first stitch. Customers would call, but he'd make excuses. He felt a profound, unshakeable guilt. Why had he been arguing about lace while the woman at the fruit stand next to him, the one who always saved him the sweetest mangoes, had been taken? The question looped endlessly in his mind, a self-inflicted torture with no answer.

Now, at 33, Kofi's world has shrunk to the four walls of his room. He rarely leaves the house. He feels disconnected from his family, watching their lives move forward from behind a thick wall of glass. He is single, having pushed away the few people who tried to get close, convinced he is a ghost, contaminated by what he witnessed. The sewing machine, his former source of pride and purpose, sits in the corner under a dusty cloth, a silent monument to the man he used to be. Most days, he just sits by the window, ever vigilant, scanning the street for threats that only he can see, a prisoner in a life he was lucky to keep.
